author: Living next to the Grump
title: Living next to the Grump
text:
The Weight He Carries

Ethan

Iwonder if she’ll still be here when I return.If the quiet between us this morning meant goodbye, or just not yet.


She didn’t answer.


But she stayed. That’s something.


It’s the day before I leave. My suitcase sits near the door, zipped and ready.


Inside, the house is quiet. Too quiet. Mia’s asleep upstairs, finally calm after a hard night. Sophie’s in the kitchen preparing her coffee. Margot moving around behind her, doing the chores, wiping down the counters, rinsing dishes in the sink. I can hear the clink of plates and the low hum of running water. Normal sounds. Familiar.


I double-check the suitcase again, even though I already went through it twice. Shirts, ties, laptop, charger, notes for the pitch. It all fits, but somehow, it still feels like I’m forgetting something.


My chest tightens.


This is the longest I’ve ever been away since Mia came into my care. One week. Maybe more. If the meeting goes well, I’ll stay a few extra days to tour the investors’ development sites. If it doesn’t… I’ll come back and try to salvage what’s left.


The truth? I’m terrified either way.


I walk to Mia’s room, careful not to wake her. Her little form is curled up in bed, arms wrapped around the worn bunny I bought her the week she arrived. Her mouth moves in her sleep. Maybe dreaming, maybe just murmuring.


Her routines are still fragile. We’ve worked hard to build them, and she leans so much on consistency. One missed step, one unexpected change, and everything spirals.


And I’m about to leave.


I lean on the doorframe, guilt pressing down like weights stacked on my shoulders.


What kind of father leaves when his kid is still unraveling?


But I don’t have a choice.


I tried to delay this meeting twice already. They won’t wait again. If I don’t secure the funding, the business folds. That means layoffs. That means walking away from something I’ve spent years building. That means I fail, not just Mia, but the people who’ve stood by me.


I close her door gently and head downstairs.


The scent of toast and coffee floats through the hallway.


Sophie’s at the table, her hair in a loose braid over one shoulder, flipping through Mia’s visual schedule. Her movements are quiet, mechanical.


Mia’s colored tabs are spread across the table, all carefully arranged, but there’s tension in the way she holds her pen, like she’s gripping it too tightly.


Her jaw is tight, her eyes flicking over the schedule like she’s trying to concentrate but keeps losing the thread.


There’s a heaviness in her posture, like she’s bracing herself for something she doesn’t want to face. And I know I’m the reason for that weight today.


I hover in the doorway, unsure how to even begin.


“I wouldn’t ask if I had any other option,” I say quietly.


She doesn’t speak.


“Miss Dana’s great, but Mia cries the second I’m gone. And Margot…” I glance toward the window. “She means well, but she still doesn’t get it. She pushes too hard.”


I hear the back door click shut as Margot steps outside, probably off to tend the garden or hang the laundry. She’s always busy, always moving, but never quite tuned in to what Mia really needs.


I run a hand through my hair. “Mia won’t talk to them. She won’t eat with them. You’re the only one she lets close.”


Sophie looks away.


I take a step toward her, then stop. “I know this isn’t fair to ask. But I need someone here who understands her. Someone she trusts.”


Still nothing.


“I’m begging you,” I say. “Just until I get back. A week, maybe more. "I just... I can’t do this unless I know she’s okay."


Silence.


Sophie exhales slowly, then leans her weight on the edge of the island, fingers gripping the marble counter. Her eyes stay fixed on the floor, lashes lowered, like looking at me might make this harder. Her shoulders rise with the breath she takes, and then fall.


She nods. Just once.


Not for me. Not even for herself.


But for Mia.


That one tiny nod feels like a lifeline and a gut punch all at once.


I swallow the lump in my throat and whisper, “Thank you.”


I know she didn’t have to say yes. I know she’s already done more than I deserve.


She doesn’t say anything.


She doesn’t ask questions right away. Just listens.


I run a hand through my hair, already tired and the day’s just begun. “It’s not a regular pitch. It’s a partnership meeting. This guy, Franklin, runs a small tech investment group. If he likes what I show him, he’ll fund our next phase. If not…”


I shake my head.


Sophie’s voice is quiet, but there’s a slight tremble behind it. “You’re falling apart.”


She blinks quickly, like she’s trying not to show how much it gets to her. Her fingers twist around each other in her lap, and for the first time, I see the uncertainty in her eyes. Not because she doesn’t believe in me, but because she knows what this cost looks like.


I don’t answer. I don’t have to.


She leans back slightly, her arms crossing in front of her. “How bad is it?”


I let out a slow breath. “We’re bleeding, Sophie. I’ve done everything I can to hold it together, but these past two years… I wasn’t prepared.”


Flashbacks crowd my head:


Nights at the office with nothing but vending machine coffee, the silence after I told two long-time employees I couldn’t afford to keep them on, watching quarterly reports dip lower with each passing month.


And still… I never regretted choosing Mia.


She came first.


Always.


But now, I’m running out of ways to bandage the wound. The business won’t survive another year unless I do something drastic.


Sophie doesn’t interrupt. She just… stays. Present. Steady.


I glance at her again. The way she sits across from me, calm and focused. Not judging. Not panicking.


“She trusts you,” I say before I can stop myself.


Sophie looks down at the coloring book on the table. “I trust her, too.”


That hits harder than I expected.


The silence between us stretches again, not heavy this time, but thoughtful.


“I hate this,” I admit. “Leaving.”


“I know.”


I lower my gaze. “What if it’s a setback for her? What if she shuts down again? What if it undoes everything we’ve worked for?”


Sophie rests her hands on the table. “You’ve done everything you can to prepare her.”


I shake my head. “It’s not enough.”


She meets my eyes. “It’s more than most would even attempt.”


Her voice is soft but sure. I believe her. Even if I don’t believe in myself.


I rise from the table.


I pass the sunroom and stop short.


At some point while I was pacing through the house, Mia must’ve woken up and come downstairs. She’s now sitting on a thick blanket on the floor, small bins of dried beans, foam shapes, and rice scattered around her. Sophie kneels beside her, guiding her hands through the textures.


Mia giggles.


It’s soft. Light. Real.


Sophie smiles, brushing a strand of hair from Mia’s face. The late morning sun slants through the windows, wrapping them in gold. For a second, it looks like a life I don’t belong in. Like something borrowed.


But I want it anyway.


—


That night, after dinner and bath time, after Mia’s finally tucked in with her bunny and her storytime playlist humming from the tablet, I sit on the back porch with Sophie.


The air is cool, the stars peeking through the inky sky. Crickets hum, and the world feels still.


I stare ahead, watching the dark line where sky meets trees.


“I don’t know who I am outside of responsibility,” I say.


Sophie doesn’t speak at first. I feel her shift beside me, maybe turning toward me, maybe not.


She draws her knees to her chest, arms wrapping around them like she’s holding something in. I glance her way. Her mouth opens slightly, but whatever she meant to say, she swallows it back. Her expression is unreadable, but there’s something in her eyes. Like she’s been there too, buried under the weight of everyone else’s needs.


She exhales slowly, and it sounds more like a surrender than anything else. I want to ask what she’s thinking, what she’s feeling, but I don’t. Because I already know.


“You’ve taken on too much,” she says finally, her voice barely above a whisper. “You carry everything and still act like you’re supposed to be okay.”


I let out a soft breath. “Someone has to be steady.”


She turns to face me, her eyes meeting mine in the dark. “But who’s steady for you?”


I’m not sure how to answer that. I never had an answer. Until now.


“You’ve been that person,” I say, the words falling more easily than I expected. “For Mia. For me. Even when I’ve been impossible to deal with.”


Sophie’s lips curve slightly, not quite a smile, but close. “You’re not impossible.”


“Tell that to the version of me two months ago,” I say with a soft chuckle.


We sit there for a long moment, the silence finally feeling safe.


“Thank you,” I murmur. “For staying. For showing up even when you didn’t have to.”


She leans her shoulder gently into mine. “You’re welcome.”


It lingers between us, not just the words, but the feeling that maybe, just maybe, I’m not alone in this.


—


The next morning comes too fast.


I dress in silence, careful not to wake the house. The suitcase is waiting at the door, zipped and ready.


As I reach for the handle, I hear soft footsteps.


Mia.


She sees me and freezes, eyes wide.


Then she runs. Clings to my leg like a lifeline, burying her face against my jeans.


“Don’t go, Daddy,” she says, her voice breaking. “Please don’t go.”


My heart cracks.


I kneel, arms wrapping around her tightly.


“I’ll be back,” I whisper, throat thick. “I promise.”


Sophie appears in the hallway, her face still sleepy but calm.


She moves to us, crouching down. “Sweetheart, remember what we talked about? We’re going to keep doing our fun mornings. We’ll color, and we’ll build the train track. You’ll show Daddy everything when he comes back, right?”


Mia sniffles. She doesn’t answer. But her grip loosens just slightly.


I rise slowly, brushing my hand through her hair. Sophie holds her hand gently, grounding her.


Our eyes meet.


Everything I want to say gets stuck in my throat.


But I manage one thing.


“When I come back… will you still be here?”


Sophie doesn’t answer.
